Subject: Post-demo: Performance SLOs & autoscaling questions

Hi Marissa —

Thanks again for the demo earlier. A few follow-up items from our engineering and SRE teams so we can qualify performance for our procurement cycle: 

- Latency SLOs: we want to understand 95th pct request latency expectations for both non-streaming and streaming flows. For streaming specifically, time-to-first-byte (TTFB) is a hard requirement — target TTFB < 200ms at 95th under normal load.
- Throughput & concurrency: baseline steady concurrency ~500 concurrent requests (mostly short chat interactions). Peak bursts can hit ~1,500 concurrent sessions for 10–15 minutes during business spikes.
- Scale-up & warm pools: how quickly can Redwood scale from zero to capacity for a new private deploy? We need an expected scale-up time and options for warm pools/pre-warmed workers to handle bursts.
- Queueing & backpressure: what happens when concurrency > provisioned capacity? Are requests queued, rejected, or routed to lower-tier model variants?
- SLA credits & penalties: brief confirmation on what latency degradations qualify for credits (this will go to our procurement).

Can you (or someone from your infra team) share a quick summary for the above and propose next steps? Happy to run a short workload test if that helps.

Thanks,
Sam
Sam Patel
Head of Platform Engineering, FinPay

From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>

Cc: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek@redwood.ai>, David Kim <david@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-02-22T17:22:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Post-demo: Performance SLOs & autoscaling questions

Sam —

Great questions, thanks for laying them out. See answers inline and next steps below. I attached our standard SLO & autoscaling template (redwood-slo-template.pdf) which we can fill out with your numbers.

- Latency SLOs: For non-streaming requests we typically size for 95p <= 300ms for short responses on our dedicated configs. For streaming, our TTFB at 95p depends on model & sequence length; for the Llama-2-Chat family on Dedicated we commonly hit ~120–220ms TTFB with an idle warm pool. We can target your 200ms 95p as a goal for the pilot.
- Throughput & concurrency: Baseline 500 concurrent is well within our Dedicated profile. For 1,500 concurrent short sessions we recommend burst capacity + warm pool strategy (details below).
- Scale-up & warm pools: Options: 1) pre-warmed pool (recommended) — keeps N workers hot and ready, giving sub-200s time-to-first-request; 2) cold scale with autoscaler — typical cold-start scale-up ~3–7 minutes depending on model and infra region.
- Queueing & backpressure: Redwood supports priority queues + configurable backpressure. If capacity is exceeded we can queue requests (with configurable queue depth and customer-visible 429s) or route to a lower-cost variant automatically as a fallback.
- SLA credits: I'll loop in legal/CS for formal language, but we can share our standard SLA matrix and credit triggers.

Next steps:
1) Vivek/David to confirm recommended warm-pool sizing and any constraints for FinPay's expected burst profile.
2) Schedule a 2-hour load run with FinPay to validate 95p TTFB and scale behavior.
3) Fill the attached template and return — we'll use it to produce a proposed config and cost estimate.

Vivek/David — can you weigh in on warm pool sizing and an internal runbook we can share with Sam?

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Senior Account Exec, Redwood Inference

On Mon, Feb 22, 2026 at 5:22 PM Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai> wrote:
> Vivek/David — can you weigh in on warm pool sizing and an internal runbook we can share with Sam?

Hi all — quick technical summary from infra: 

- Warm pool approach: we recommend a pre-warmed pool sized to absorb the first 10–20% of peak burst without scaling (so for 1,500 concurrent peak, keep ~150–300 pre-warmed workers). Each worker supports ~8–12 short chat sessions depending on model tokenization; we can provide a model-specific mapping in the template.
- Scale-up time: with warm pool we see time-to-capacity for the remaining burst in ~60–180s (depends on cloud instance boot/driver load and model init). Cold starts (no warm pool) can be 3–7 minutes for large models.
- Queueing behavior: Redwood's request router uses a token-bucket for each route + prioritized queues per customer tier. When capacity exceeded: 1) short queue (configurable, default 30s), 2) if queue > threshold, requests receive a 429 with retry-after. We also support automatic fallback to a quantized or cheaper model variant (configurable).
- Observability & telemetry: we will surface time-to-first-byte (TTFB), time-to-last-token, per-route queue depth, per-worker warm/cold state, and autoscaler events in the Console for the pilot.

Attachments: warm-pool-arch.png (simple diagram of warm pool + autoscaler + queueing)

Proposal: schedule a 2-hour load validation Wednesday 2026-02-25 09:00–11:00 PT. Goals: validate 95p TTFB < 200ms during steady/peak and confirm total scale-up time <3 minutes to handle 1,500 concurrent burst with targeted warm pool.

Happy to join the run and iterate on warm pool size once we see real traffic.

—Vivek
Vivek Kulkarni
Head of Infra, Redwood Inference
